subsection: 13. The impact of advances in the biological sciences, nuclear power and the computer

notes.h: Background: why science and technology mattered after 1945
notes.b: Three advances, in biology and medicine, nuclear power and the computer, reshaped Europe after 1945. They grew out of the war and the Cold War, so their causes need to be clear before the detail.
points: The Second World War drove research, because governments paid for anything that might win the war: penicillin, radar, code-breaking and the atomic bomb all came from wartime work. The atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

Post-war reconstruction and the welfare state (government-funded health and social care), such as the National Health Service that began in Britain in 1948, made new treatments available to ordinary people, not only the rich.

The Cold War, the rivalry between the Western and Soviet blocs, pushed both sides to compete in science and technology, and each side held nuclear weapons. This is why nuclear technology and computing both began as military projects.
The oil crisis of 1973, when oil prices rose sharply, made governments seek energy independence, which is why many turned to nuclear power.
Information technology (IT) is the use of computers and electronic systems to store, process and transmit information. It became central to the economy in these decades.
notes.tip: Exams ask for dated examples from all three fields, so use this background to link them to the war and the Cold War.

notes.b: Before 1945 infections such as pneumonia and tuberculosis (TB) were major killers. Antibiotics (drugs that kill bacteria) and vaccines (which train the body to resist a disease) changed that.
points: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain led the Oxford team that turned it into a usable drug, with work from about 1939 to 1941.
Penicillin was mass-produced mainly in the USA in 1943-44, because Britain could not spare the industrial capacity in wartime. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.
Streptomycin, discovered in 1943 in the laboratory of Selman Waksman in the USA, was the first effective drug against tuberculosis.
Antibiotics were used widely in the 1950s, which cut deaths from bacterial infections such as pneumonia and TB in Western Europe, and TB deaths fell sharply.
Jonas Salk's injected polio vaccine was announced on 12 April 1955. Albert Sabin's oral vaccine, easier to give, was widely used from the early 1960s.
Vaccination campaigns against diphtheria, tuberculosis (the BCG vaccine, developed in France and in mass use in Europe after 1945), polio and measles reduced child deaths.
Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide by the World Health Organization in 1980, showing what vaccination could achieve.
The welfare state made new drugs and hospital treatment available to all, so life expectancy in Western Europe rose markedly between 1945 and 1990.
notes.tip: Fleming and Florey and Chain are often confused: Fleming discovered penicillin, Florey and Chain developed it into a drug, and mass production was American. Likewise Salk is the injected vaccine of 1955 and Sabin the oral one of the early 1960s. Give the date with each.

notes.h: Medicine: the pill, transplants and surgery
notes.b: Alongside drugs, new medical technology let doctors replace organs, support failing ones and look inside the body.
points: The oral contraceptive pill, approved in the USA in 1960, spread through Western Europe in the 1960s. It is a medical advance with social effects, giving people more control over reproduction.
The first successful kidney transplant, between identical twins, took place in Boston in 1954. Identical twins were used because their matching tissue lowers the risk of the body rejecting the organ.
The first human heart transplant was performed by Christiaan Barnard in Cape Town on 3 December 1967. It took place in South Africa, so use it as an example of a medical advance, not a European one.

The heart pacemaker (first implanted in Sweden in 1958) and kidney dialysis (a machine that cleans the blood, developed by Willem Kolff in the Netherlands in the 1940s) kept patients alive whose organs were failing.
Hip replacements were developed by John Charnley in England in the 1960s, and Godfrey Hounsfield developed the CT scanner, which builds images of the body from X-rays, in 1971.
notes.tip: For a 40-mark paragraph on medicine, name the advance, the person, the date and its effect on health, for example the 1954 kidney transplant or the polio vaccine.

notes.b: DNA is the molecule that carries genetic instructions. Once its structure was known, scientists could read it and begin to change it, and this opened the way to genetic engineering (altering an organism's genes).
points: James Watson and Francis Crick, at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, published the double-helix model of DNA in April 1953.

The X-ray evidence came from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King's College London. Franklin's X-ray photograph, Photo 51, was taken in 1952, and Wilkins showed it to Watson in early 1953, so her data reached them through Wilkins, not from Franklin herself.
Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958 and the prize is not awarded after death, so she was not included.
In 1973 Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer in the USA demonstrated recombinant DNA techniques, which join DNA from different organisms and so allow genes to be moved between them.
In 1977 Frederick Sanger at Cambridge developed a method of DNA sequencing, reading the order of the chemical units that make up a gene.

Genetically engineered human insulin made by bacteria, in the USA in 1978, was the first of the genetically engineered drugs. The biotechnology industry, which sells products made with living cells, grew in the 1980s.
The first in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) baby, Louise Brown, was born in Oldham, England, on 25 July 1978 after work by Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe. IVF is fertilising an egg outside the body.
notes.tip: DNA 1953 and IVF 1978 are among the most-tested dates. Remember that Franklin's evidence reached Watson and Crick through Wilkins, and explain why she did not share the 1962 prize.

notes.h: Ethics, risks and regulation in biology
notes.b: Each advance brought new risks and moral questions, and governments responded with regulation. Examiners reward answers that set these problems against the benefits.
points: The thalidomide scandal showed the risks. The drug was sold in West Germany from 1957 as a sedative and for morning sickness, and caused birth defects in thousands of children. It was withdrawn in 1961, and this led to stricter drug testing and regulation.

The ethics of IVF, embryo research and genetic engineering were debated. The Warnock Report in Britain in 1984 recommended regulation, and the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act followed in Britain in 1990.
The Catholic Church opposed IVF, a view set out in a Vatican instruction of 1987.
DNA fingerprinting, which identifies people from their DNA, was developed by Alec Jeffreys at Leicester in 1984 and first used in a British murder inquiry in 1986.
Debates about genetic engineering, embryo research and drug safety led governments to set up regulatory bodies and ethics committees in the 1980s.
The effects were mixed: better health and longer lives, but also unequal access to treatment, new costs and moral questions.
notes.tip: Pair benefits with problems: cures and longer lives against thalidomide and the ethics of IVF.

notes.h: Nuclear power: from weapons to electricity
notes.b: The atomic bomb of 1945 showed the power of the atom. In the 1950s governments turned the same science towards electricity, promoting it as a source of cheap energy and a peaceful use of nuclear technology.
points: Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace speech to the UN in December 1953 promoted civil nuclear power, and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was founded in 1957.
CERN, the European Organisation for Nuclear Research, was founded at Geneva in 1954 by twelve European states for cooperative physics research. It was not a power programme.
The Treaty of Rome of 1957 created Euratom, which coordinated nuclear energy in the six EEC states, so no state had to develop it alone.
Obninsk in the USSR supplied electricity to a public grid from June 1954, the first nuclear plant connected to a public network.
Calder Hall in Cumbria, England, opened in October 1956 and was the first nuclear power station to supply electricity on a commercial scale. It also produced plutonium for weapons.
Nuclear deterrence, the idea that weapons prevent war because an enemy fears retaliation, was the military side of the same technology, and stockpiles grew on both sides.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Obninsk (first connected to a public grid, 1954) with Calder Hall (first commercial scale, 1956), or CERN, the IAEA and Euratom. Keep civil nuclear power separate from nuclear weapons.

notes.h: Nuclear power: expansion and the French programme
notes.b: The oil crisis of 1973 turned nuclear power from an option into a priority for governments that wanted energy independence.
points: The Messmer Plan of 1974 committed France to a large reactor-building programme, so the country would not depend on imported oil. Nuclear power supplied about three quarters of French electricity by the 1990s.
After 1973 West Germany, Sweden, the USSR and others also expanded their nuclear programmes.
The USSR built reactors across the bloc, including the RBMK reactors (a Soviet design) used at Chernobyl.
The Windscale fire in Cumbria in October 1957 was Britain's worst nuclear accident and released radioactive iodine over the countryside, an early warning of the risks.
notes.tip: For short answers, know what the Messmer Plan committed France to and the 1974 date. Always say 'about' and 'by the 1990s' for the French share.

notes.b: As nuclear power and nuclear weapons spread, so did opposition. Campaigners feared accidents, radioactive waste and nuclear war, and they used marches, protests and referendums.
points: The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) was founded in Britain in 1958 and organised the Aldermaston marches, using the peace symbol designed in 1958.
Greenpeace was founded in 1971 in Vancouver, Canada, and campaigned against nuclear testing and nuclear power.

The Three Mile Island accident in Pennsylvania, USA, on 28 March 1979 was a partial reactor meltdown. It was the worst accident in US commercial nuclear history, and no new US reactor orders followed for many years.
Anti-nuclear protests in West Germany, Britain and the Netherlands grew in the early 1980s, alongside protests against NATO missile deployment.
In Ireland a plan for a nuclear plant at Carnsore Point, Co. Wexford, was shelved after large protests in the late 1970s, and the plant was never built.
Austria's Zwentendorf plant, completed in 1978, never operated because a referendum in November 1978 rejected it. Sweden held a referendum on nuclear power in 1980.
notes.tip: Know Three Mile Island (1979, USA), Chernobyl (1986, USSR) and Windscale (1957, Britain) apart. The anti-nuclear movement here means protest against nuclear power, not green politics in general.

notes.b: Chernobyl was the worst nuclear accident in Europe. It showed that the effects of a reactor failure cross borders, and it changed policy in both East and West.
points: On 26 April 1986 a reactor at Chernobyl in Soviet Ukraine exploded during a safety test, helped by design flaws in the RBMK reactor.
Radioactive material spread across Europe in a cloud. The town of Pripyat nearby was evacuated, and a 30-kilometre exclusion zone was created around the plant.
The Soviet authorities were slow to admit the accident. An announcement came on 28 April, only after Swedish monitors detected the radioactive cloud.
Large numbers of people were evacuated and resettled. The health effects are disputed and estimates of deaths vary widely.
Chernobyl led to closer international cooperation on safety. Some see the secrecy around it as exposing the weakness of the Soviet system.

In Western Europe it prompted a re-think. Italy voted in 1987 to end nuclear power, and the accidents together meant tighter safety, slower growth of nuclear power and a continuing debate on risks and waste.
notes.tip: If asked about Chernobyl, give the date, the causes (safety test plus RBMK design flaws), the cloud, the Soviet delay and the evacuation. Give no death toll, because estimates vary.

notes.h: The development of the computer: early machines
notes.b: Modern computers grew out of wartime code-breaking and a run of hardware advances, each making machines smaller, cheaper and more reliable.
points: Alan Turing's theoretical paper of 1936 laid the foundations of computing.
Colossus, built at Bletchley Park in 1943-44 by a team under Tommy Flowers, broke German teleprinter codes. It was programmable and electronic but not general-purpose.
ENIAC, completed in the USA in 1945, was a general-purpose electronic digital computer, meaning it could be set to many different tasks.
The Manchester Baby of June 1948 was the first stored-program computer to run, meaning it held its instructions in memory.
The transistor, invented at Bell Laboratories in the USA in December 1947, replaced bulky vacuum tubes, so computers became smaller and cheaper.

The integrated circuit, or microchip, packs many components onto one small slice of material. Jack Kilby developed it in 1958 and Robert Noyce in 1959, and the Intel 4004 microprocessor, a whole processor on one chip, followed in 1971.
notes.tip: Keep early machines apart: Colossus (code-breaking, 1943-44), ENIAC (1945), Manchester Baby (1948). Likewise transistor 1947, integrated circuit 1958-59, microprocessor 1971. The transistor made computers smaller and cheaper.

notes.b: Computers first served governments and big companies, and then reached homes. Networks then linked them together.
points: A mainframe is a large, powerful computer used by government and business. LEO, built for J. Lyons and Co. (the Lyons tea shops) in Britain in 1951, was the first business computer.
IBM's System/360 mainframe, launched in 1964, set the standard for business computing in Europe and the USA, and IBM dominated the mainframe market.
Minicomputers and microprocessors from the 1970s made computing cheaper. A personal computer is one designed for a single user at home or in the office.

The Apple II of 1977 and the IBM Personal Computer, launched on 12 August 1981, spread personal computing into offices and homes in the 1980s. The Sinclair ZX Spectrum of 1982 was a cheap British home micro.
In France the Minitel online terminal was launched in 1982, and terminals were distributed free or cheaply to telephone subscribers, so many households were online early.
ARPANET, a US network, was first connected in 1969 and became the basis of the internet. Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989, and it was launched publicly in 1991.
notes.tip: Distinguish the internet (ARPANET, 1969) from the World Wide Web (proposed at CERN in 1989, public in 1991). The IBM PC of 1981 is one of the most-tested anchors.

notes.h: Effects of computers on work and everyday life
notes.b: Computers could do routine tasks faster and more cheaply than people, which changed the kind of work Europeans did.
points: Computers automated routine office and factory work, so demand fell for some clerical and manufacturing jobs in Western Europe.
Automation reduced employment in manufacturing, while service jobs in banking, insurance and administration grew. This contributed to deindustrialisation, the decline of heavy industry.
Banks introduced cash machines from 1967, with the first in Britain that year. Supermarkets adopted bar codes in the 1970s, and word processors and spreadsheets spread through offices in the 1980s.
Information technology became a key concept in the economy, and the pace of change in the 1980s prepared the ground for the global networks that followed.
notes.tip: Effects questions reward two-sided answers: automation destroyed clerical and factory jobs but created service and technology jobs. Name the advance, the person, the date and the effect on jobs.

notes.b: Computing and microelectronics became part of the East-West contest, because advanced technology gave economic and military strength.
points: Western export controls, coordinated through COCOM (the coordinating committee for export controls, set up in 1949), restricted the sale of advanced computing technology to the Soviet bloc.
The Soviet bloc fell behind the West in computing and electronics, a gap that Soviet planners tried to close through copying and espionage.
By the 1980s Soviet leaders recognised that the Soviet Union lagged badly in computing and microelectronics, which was one of the reasons for the push for economic reform.
Europe lagged behind the USA and Japan in computing and electronics, so the EEC launched ESPRIT, a research programme in information technology, in 1984.
notes.tip: Link the Cold War to all three fields: nuclear technology came from weapons research, COCOM restricted computing technology, and Soviet failure to keep up fed pressure for reform.

notes.b: Historians and contemporaries have judged these advances by the benefits they brought and by the new dangers and inequalities they created.
points: Achievements: longer life expectancy, the control of infectious disease, cheap electricity from nuclear plants, better communication and higher productivity from computers.

Limits: nuclear accidents, the risks of radioactive waste, the ethical questions raised by reproductive and genetic technology, job losses from automation, unequal access to new treatments and Europe's dependence on the USA and Japan for technology.

Contemporaries in the 1950s often celebrated science as the key to progress, while the anti-nuclear and environmental movements of the 1970s and 1980s, and accidents such as Three Mile Island and Chernobyl, challenged that view.
Later historians stress that the impact of these technologies depended on political decisions about how they were used, not only on their scientific potential.

On which had the greatest impact on Europeans by 1992, the case for medicine is that it touched every life through health and longer lives. The case for the computer is that it changed work and daily life. Nuclear power mattered most in France but was checked by accidents.
notes.tip: The 100-mark essay asks you to assess the significance of all three advances. Make a judgement on which had most impact, with dated examples from all three fields, and pair benefits with problems in each. An answer on only one or two fields scores poorly.

keyTerms.definition: The use of computers and electronic systems to store, process and transmit information, which transformed work and communication after 1945.
The strategy of preventing attack by possessing nuclear weapons able to inflict unacceptable damage on an aggressor.
The technique of altering the genetic material of an organism, first demonstrated in 1973 through recombinant DNA methods.
A small integrated circuit that combines many electronic components on one piece of semiconductor material, enabling the modern computer.
A large computer used by businesses and governments for data processing from the 1950s to the 1970s.
The campaign against nuclear weapons and nuclear power, which grew in the 1970s and 1980s.
DNA made by joining genetic material from different organisms, first achieved in the early 1970s, the basis of genetic engineering.
The nuclear reactor in Soviet Ukraine that exploded on 26 April 1986, causing the worst nuclear accident in history.
A computer small and cheap enough to be bought by individuals, spreading from the late 1970s.
